blocks.prompt: The Beaver That Builds Its Own Pond
blocks.text: A beaver's front teeth never stop growing. They are orange, and they are as sharp as a chisel. The beaver leans against a tree and gnaws around and around until the tree falls. Then it drags the branches into the stream. It pushes sticks and mud together until the water backs up and spreads out into a pond. In the middle of the pond the beaver builds a lodge. The only doors are under the water, so a wolf cannot get in. Inside, above the water line, there is a dry room with a floor of soft wood chips. That is where the beaver family sleeps.

blocks.prompt: Why the Beaver Builds
blocks.text: A beaver does not eat wood. It eats the soft living layer just under the bark, plus leaves and water plants. So why does it cut down whole trees? The answer is water. A beaver on land is slow and clumsy. A beaver in water is quick and safe. So the beaver makes more water. It drags branches into a stream and packs them with mud until the flow stops and a pond spreads out behind the wall. Now the beaver can swim almost everywhere it needs to go. In the pond it piles up a lodge of sticks and mud. Every door is underwater. Above the water line it hollows out a dry room, and that is where the family sleeps through the winter. Before the ice comes, the beaver shoves fresh branches into the mud at the bottom of the pond. When the pond freezes over, it swims down under the ice and brings a stick back up to chew. Its food is in the cellar. Scientists have even learned what tells a beaver to start building. It is the sound of running water. A beaver hears trickling and begins stacking sticks.

blocks.prompt: The Animal That Builds Rivers
blocks.text: Most animals fit themselves to the world they find. The beaver rebuilds the world to fit itself. A beaver is a rodent, the second largest in the world after the capybara, and almost every part of its body is built for water. Its back feet are webbed like a duck's. Its tail is flat and scaly and works as a rudder. A clear third eyelid slides across each eye like a swim mask. Its lips seal shut behind its front teeth, so it can carry a branch through the water without swallowing a mouthful. It can hold its breath for several minutes at a time. Those front teeth are the tools. They never stop growing, and the front face of each tooth is coated in enamel hardened with iron, which is what turns it orange. The back of the tooth is softer. As the beaver gnaws, the soft side wears away faster and leaves a chisel edge, so every bite sharpens the blade again. With that chisel the beaver cuts trees, and with the trees it builds a dam. The dam stops a stream and floods the land behind it. That flood is the whole point. Deep water means safe travel and a lodge no wolf can enter. But the pond does far more than shelter one family. It slows the current so silt settles out. It soaks the ground so the valley stays damp through a dry summer. It makes still, sunny shallows where frogs, fish, ducks, and insects can live. Trees that drown at the edge become nest holes for woodpeckers. Ecologists have a name for an animal that changes a place so much that other species come to depend on the change. They call it a keystone species.

notes: Castor canadensis and Castor fiber

blocks.prompt: The Fur That Emptied a Continent
blocks.text: Before Europeans arrived, tens of millions of beavers lived in North America. Nobody can give an exact figure, because nobody counted them, but the shape of the continent recorded them. Beaver dams stood on nearly every stream from the northern tree line down into Mexico. The valleys behind those dams were not the tidy single rivers we picture today. They were staircases of ponds, meadows, and marsh: wet, slow, and crowded with life. Then hats happened. Beaver underfur is covered in microscopic barbs, and when it is pressed and heated it locks together into felt that is dense, waterproof, and almost indestructible. For roughly two hundred years, a felt beaver hat was the thing a European gentleman was expected to own. Europe had already trapped out its own beavers. North America had not. What followed was one of the largest wildlife harvests in history. Trading companies pushed west along the rivers, and the beaver became money. In some regions, trappers deliberately cleared every animal from a valley to make the land worthless to rivals. By 1900 the North American beaver, once counted in the tens of millions, was down to perhaps one hundred thousand. The Eurasian beaver was down to around twelve hundred animals, scattered in a few small pockets. The water changed with them. Without dams, the ponds drained. Without ponds, wet meadows dried and hardened, and streams cut down into narrow channels that flushed rain straight toward the sea. People who arrived later looked at those fast, tidy channels and assumed they had always been there. An entire landscape had been quietly deleted, and almost nobody noticed the connection. The ending is better than it should be. Fashion moved on to silk, trapping laws arrived, and beavers were carried back into empty valleys. Idaho went as far as dropping them into the backcountry by parachute in 1948. Ten to fifteen million now live in North America. In some places they flood roads and fell prized trees, and people argue about them bitterly. In others, land managers pay to put beavers back, because a beaver builds flood control and drought insurance for free.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Castor canadensis, the second largest rodent alive
Iron-reinforced enamel: hard, orange, self-sharpening
Lars Wilsson, 1960s: beavers dam the sound of running water
Beaver dam analogs are human-built starter dams
Pond levelers drain a dam quietly so it is not repaired
Emily Fairfax: beaver ponds stay green through wildfire

blocks.prompt: The Engineer We Erased, and Then Hired Back
blocks.text: There is an animal that solves problems humans spend millions of dollars on, and for two centuries we killed it for hats. Start with the body. A beaver is a rodent, second in size only to the capybara, and it is assembled almost entirely for water. Webbed hind feet drive it forward. A flat scaly tail steers it, stores fat for winter, and slaps the surface as an alarm. A transparent membrane slides across each eye so it can see while submerged. Its lips close behind the incisors, which lets it gnaw and haul timber underwater without drowning itself. The incisors are the famous part. They grow continuously, and their front face is armored with enamel reinforced by iron, which both hardens the tooth and stains it orange. Because the softer backing wears faster than the armored face, every bite resharpens the chisel. The beaver never has to stop for a whetstone. The behavior is stranger than the anatomy. In the 1960s the Swedish researcher Lars Wilsson played recordings of running water to captive beavers. They piled sticks and mud onto the loudspeaker. The animals were not reasoning about hydrology. They were answering a sound. Out of that simple rule comes a dam, and out of the dam comes a pond, and out of the pond comes a world. Consider what the pond does. It raises the water table, so the surrounding soil stays damp deep into a drought. It slows floodwater, releasing it over weeks instead of hours. It drops silt and traps fertilizer washing off farmland, so water leaves cleaner than it arrived. It creates still, sunlit shallows where amphibians breed and young fish fatten. Trees that drown at the margin become nest holes. Ecologists call a species like this a keystone: pull it out and the arch collapses. We pulled it out. Beaver felt made the hat Europe insisted on wearing, and Europe had already exhausted its own supply. Trading companies mapped a continent in pursuit of the animal. Populations once estimated in the tens of millions fell to perhaps one hundred thousand by 1900, and the Eurasian beaver was reduced to roughly twelve hundred individuals. Along with the animals went their water. Braided, swampy, pond-stepped valleys drained and hardened into single fast channels. Later generations looked at those channels and called them natural. The correction is underway, and it is unsentimental. Beavers have been reintroduced across Britain and Europe. In the American West, agencies now install beaver dam analogs, which are hand-built imitations of a beaver dam, hoping that real beavers move in and take over the maintenance. The reasoning is arithmetic. A concrete flood-control structure is expensive and needs engineers. A beaver colony works for bark. Research by the geoscientist Emily Fairfax has shown that beaver-dammed stretches of stream stay green through wildfires that burn the valley around them, because the pond keeps the ground too wet to carry flame. None of this makes the beaver easy to live with. It floods roads, it drops the ornamental tree you liked, and it does not negotiate. Where a dam threatens property, managers often fit a pond leveler, a pipe run through the dam that lowers the water quietly enough that the beaver never hears a leak to repair. That fix tells you everything. We are not persuading the animal. We are working around a rule written into it long before we arrived, and we are finally doing the math on what that rule was worth.
